name: Fatima Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Fatima. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. What's a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach computer science at Hillcrest Academy, a secondary school on the edge of the city, and I'm in my second year. Most days it's four lessons, Year 7 up to Year 11, plus the coding club at lunch on Wednesdays. I love the bit when a Year 8 gets their first game working and the whole row crowds round. I'm honestly still bad at pacing, I plan too much and run out of time, and my Year 10 group walks all over me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my friend Noor from university. I've got about ten months of money saved, mostly in an index fund, and I do two evenings a week of online coding tutoring, which pays well. I use AI every single day: lesson plans, worksheets, debugging kids' code. I'm a union member and I lean left, but I'm not scared of tech, which makes me a bit odd in the staffroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's still a great tool, it just isn't magic. I'd keep showing colleagues how I use it to make worksheets in five minutes. Online I'd probably push back on people saying AI was useless, because it isn't useless for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. My job stays, my tutoring stays, my savings keep growing. The thing I'm actually worried about is my Year 10 class and whether I pass my performance review, and AI doesn't fix a fifteen-year-old who won't sit down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for planning and spend the time I save on behaviour, maybe a course on classroom management in the spring. I'd keep tutoring two evenings and putting the extra into the index fund. I'd also run a lunchtime session for staff on using AI for worksheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little disappointed, because I like new toys, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd run a session for staff. How would that go down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of them would come for the biscuits and half would argue with me. One of the older maths teachers already calls me 'the robot girl'. But a couple would try it, and that's how it spreads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stays small, what would you want to be doing in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head of computing somewhere, probably. Or maybe I'd move into teacher training, showing new teachers how to use the tools well. I like teaching adults almost as much as kids.

say: I'd say AI is still **a great tool**, just not magic.
I'd push back online against people calling it **useless**.
think: My **job, tutoring** and savings all stay safe in this picture.
My real worry is my **Year 10 class** and passing my performance review.
do: Spend time saved by AI on a **behaviour course** in the spring.
Keep **tutoring** two evenings and add the extra to my index fund.
Run a **lunchtime session** showing staff how to make worksheets with AI.
feel: **Calm**, a little **disappointed** because I enjoy new tools.
S0.quote: AI doesn't fix a fifteen-year-old who won't sit down.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **classroom control**, not money or technology.
She's the **early adopter** in a sceptical staffroom and enjoys teaching colleagues.
Her **side tutoring** gives her both money and confidence.

steps.text: Book a classroom behaviour course for the spring term
Keep online coding tutoring two evenings a week
Run a lunchtime AI worksheet session for staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why schools need to teach kids how AI works, not ban it. I'd be the loud one asking for training budgets for staff. And I'd say the union should negotiate how the time saved is used, so it goes back to teachers, not into cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I think it's good for me. I already use the tools every day, so I'd be one of the people the school leans on. The risk is that coding is one of the things AI takes over, so parents might ask why kids should learn it at all, and computer science could shrink as a subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change my curriculum this year: less syntax drills, more how to check, test and question what an AI writes. I'd apply to be the school's AI lead, even as a junior, because nobody else wants it. I'd keep the tutoring but switch it from coding to teaching kids to use AI well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually excited. I'd be a bit worried for colleagues who hate change, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said computer science could shrink. Doesn't that touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could. If the school drops it, computer science could shrink to one GCSE group, and there's only room for one teacher, which is the head of department, not me. But I'd be teaching AI skills across subjects by then, so I'd be fine moving sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at school would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older maths teacher who calls me 'the robot girl'. He's good with kids but he does everything on paper, and he's a few years from retiring. If they bring in targets around AI use, it'd crush him.

say: I'd argue schools should **teach AI**, not ban it.
I'd press for **staff training** budgets and a union say on time saved.
think: I'd likely **gain**, because I already use the tools daily.
Computer science could **shrink as a subject** if AI does the coding.
do: Rewrite my curriculum this year around **checking and testing** AI work.
Apply to be the school's **AI lead** despite being junior.
Switch tutoring from coding to **using AI well**.
feel: **Calm** and even **excited**, with some worry for colleagues who dislike change.
S1.quote: Computer science could shrink to one GCSE group, and there's only room for one teacher, which is the head of department, not me.
fieldNote: She sees opportunity where others see threat, and is honest about her **subject shrinking**.
She'd **move sideways** into teaching AI skills across the school.
Her concern for an **older colleague** shows her progressive empathy.

steps.text: Rewrite the Year 9 course around checking AI-written code
Apply for the school's AI lead role
Relaunch tutoring as AI skills for teenagers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency government action: income support, rules for schools, and a plan for every young person leaving school into this. I'd be at the protests. I'd say it's not the tech that's the problem, it's that nobody's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think AGI by 2028 could wipe out the subject I teach. If AI does any thinking work better than a person, why would a fifteen-year-old learn Python? And the AI lead job I'd want only lasts until the AI can lead itself. The classroom part, being with kids, lasts till the robots in 2031, but it might not be a teacher's job then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell part of my index fund and keep a year's worth in cash, because markets would go mad. I'd start a part-time master's in educational psychology right away, aiming at the human side, how kids learn and feel. I'd keep tutoring as long as people still pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the one who's excited, and this is the first one that makes my stomach drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got savings and a side income. Why anxious rather than uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the tutoring and my teaching both depend on my skills. Tutoring coding dies first, because what I know is exactly what becomes cheap. Savings last a year or two, but I'm twenty-seven, I need something for the next forty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor, your flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor works in marketing, which is even more exposed than me. I'd say let's keep the flat, keep our costs low, and help each other apply for things. We'd be each other's safety net.

say: I'd demand **emergency government action**: income support, school rules and a youth plan.
I'd say the real problem is that **nobody is ready**.
think: AGI by 2028 could **wipe out** computer science as a subject.
The **classroom part** lasts till robots in 2031, but maybe not as a teacher's job.
do: Move part of my index fund into **a year of cash**.
Start a **part-time master's** in educational psychology right away.
Keep **tutoring** as long as people pay.
feel: **Anxious**, the first scenario that makes my **stomach drop**.
S2.quote: Tutoring coding dies first, because what I know is exactly what becomes cheap.
fieldNote: The early adopter feels it first: her **skills** are what AGI makes cheap.
She'd pivot to **educational psychology**, the human side of learning.
Her **flatmate** becomes her mutual safety net.

steps.text: Move part of the index fund into a year of cash
Enrol in a part-time educational psychology master's
Keep coding tutoring two evenings while demand lasts
Join protests for income support and school rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if we start now. Schools should be redesigning what they teach for a world where AI does the thinking work. I'd be writing blog posts about it and pushing my union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is decent for me. I can do the master's in educational psychology, get some experience, and be ready to move into something like learning support by 2031. Computer science as a subject probably fades, but I'd be gone from it by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the master's next September, part time, paid from my savings. I'd keep using AI heavily in class to stay sharp. And I'd slowly shift my tutoring towards study skills and confidence, which feels more human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a plan, so it's not panic, but it's a big change from what I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not leave exactly, more drift into the part of it that's about people. An educational psychologist still works with schools, just one kid at a time. I'd miss whole-class teaching, the noise of thirty kids, but I could live without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if the master's got expensive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tutoring would pay for most of it. Beyond that, I'd skip the trip to see my cousins abroad next summer. It's a big trip, about two thousand all in.

I'd blog and push my **union branch** to redesign the curriculum.

steps.text: Start the educational psychology master's next September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a huge chance to rebuild schools properly, and we should start with what kids need as people. I'd talk about it at every training day. I'd sound optimistic, because I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is great for me. I'd be thirty-seven, with a master's, years of experience, and very good with the tools. I could be the one designing how schools use AI, or working in learning support, and I'd have time to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching computer science for now and apply for head of computing in three or four years. I'd do the master's at a relaxed pace. I'd keep investing the tutoring money every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, honestly. It feels like something I could help shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about our students. The kids leaving school in 2035 will train for jobs that half-vanish by the time they're twenty. I'd want to be the teacher who tells them the truth about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change any personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd buy a flat sooner, while I'm earning well and before it all shifts. I'd also want to be settled with someone by my thirties, but that's not up to AI.

say: I'd call ten years a **huge chance** to rebuild schools properly.
I'd sound **optimistic** at every training day.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd have a master's, experience and strong AI skills.
I'd have **time to choose** between AI design and learning support.
do: Apply for **head of computing** in three or four years.
Do the **master's** at a relaxed pace.
Keep **investing** the tutoring money every month.
feel: **Calm** and **curious**, like it's something I could help shape.
S4.quote: The kids leaving school in 2035 will train for jobs that half-vanish by the time they're twenty.
fieldNote: With a decade, her **adaptability** turns into ambition.
Her worry shifts to **school leavers**, not herself.

steps.text: Apply for head of computing within four years
Invest tutoring income in the index fund each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits the exact skills I'm proud of. What would help is funded retraining for teachers, like paid master's places in psychology or special needs, and income support while people switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd tell my students. I'd tell them straight. The coding I teach might not matter, but learning to stick with a hard problem always will.

headlineQuote: The coding I teach might not matter, but learning to stick with a hard problem always will.
portrait: A **second-year** computer science teacher at a city academy, still weak on **pacing**.
Shares a flat, has **ten months' savings** and earns extra from online tutoring.
Uses AI **every day** and is the staffroom's early adopter.
Calm in slower worlds, but **AGI by 2028** hits the skills she's proudest of.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would make her coding skills **cheap** overnight.
